title: The hemispheres: lobes, proportions and the visual pathway
description: How the cortex declares itself through language, attention, gaze, the proportions of a weakness and the visual fields, and how injury early in life shapes the developing hemisphere.
why: The cortex is where localization becomes least precise and also most interesting, because a lesion there can take away abilities that no lower level of the nervous system can touch.
objectives: Recognise the signs that only a cortical lesion can produce, and use them to lift a hemiparesis to the hemisphere.
Use the proportion of face, arm and leg weakness to separate lateral cortex, medial cortex and internal capsule.
Map a visual field defect to its site, and test the fields in a child.
Separate acquired from developmental language problems, and recognise the exam patterns of perinatal brain injury.

sections.title: Cortical signatures
sections.content:
Most of the nervous system gives itself away through its wiring. In the cord and the brainstem you localize by crossings and neighbours, noting that a tract has crossed at one level and that a nucleus sits beside it at another, and the answer falls out of the geometry. The hemispheres call for a different kind of reasoning. Most of what we know about where functions live there was first learned from strokes, wounds and tumours, which Brazis calls true "experiments of Nature" (Brazis 2011, p. 493), and although imaging and cortical mapping have since refined the map, you still read it at the bedside the old way, by noticing which human abilities have gone missing.

**What only the cortex can lose**

A lesion in the cord or brainstem can weaken a hand, but only a lesion of the hemisphere can take away the ability to name that hand, to notice it, or to recognise a coin placed in it. Pearl lists the signatures of a cortical lesion (Pearl 2014, p. 108):

- **Aphasia**, from a lesion of the language-dominant hemisphere, which is the left in almost all right-handers.
- **Homonymous visual field cuts.**
- **Cortical sensory loss**, in which the touch is felt but the object goes unrecognised, two points cannot be told apart, and a number drawn on the palm cannot be read.
- **Agnosia and neglect**, classically of the left side of space after a right parietal lesion.
- **Apraxia**, in which a strong limb with normal sensation still cannot carry out a complex motor task.
- **A dissociated weakness**, with the face and arm affected differently from the leg, which the next section takes apart.

Two more signs belong with these. **Seizures** arise in the cortex, and a focal seizure is often the most precise localizing sign a child will give you. **Gaze preference** comes from the frontal eye fields, each of which drives the eyes toward the opposite side, so a destructive lesion lets the eyes drift toward the side of the lesion while a seizure drives them away from it (Pearl 2014, pp. 9-10).

**The bedside decision**

When you find a hemiparesis, the useful question is what keeps it company. Brazis gives the practical list of neighbouring signs, which are aphasia, hemisensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, unawareness of the deficit and a history of focal seizures (Brazis 2011, p. 11). Any one of them lifts the lesion into the hemisphere, whereas a pure motor hemiparesis with none of them points deeper, to the internal capsule or the brainstem (Brazis 2011, p. 12).

**In a child**

Young children cannot report most of these signatures, so you have to watch for them instead. Neglect shows up as a toddler who ignores the toys on one side, apraxia as a child who cannot copy a gesture that a younger sibling manages, and aphasia as words that were there last month and have since gone.
keyPoints: Much of cortical localization was learned from lesions and their effects, which Brazis calls "experiments of Nature" (Brazis 2011, p. 493).
The signatures of a cortical lesion include aphasia, homonymous field cuts, cortical sensory loss, neglect, apraxia and a dissociated weakness (Pearl 2014, p. 108).
A destructive frontal lesion lets the eyes drift toward the lesion, and a seizure drives them away from it (Pearl 2014, pp. 9-10).
A hemiparesis with cortical signs beside it lies in the hemisphere, while a pure motor hemiparesis points deeper (Brazis 2011, pp. 11-12).

question.question: A 10-year-old wakes with weakness of his left arm and the lower half of his face. His eyes rest looking to the right, he ignores you when you stand on his left, and he does not seem troubled by the weakness. Where is the lesion?
options: Right hemisphere, involving the frontal and parietal cortex
question.explanation: Left-sided weakness that comes with left neglect, unawareness of the deficit and a gaze preference to the right is a cortical picture from the right hemisphere. A destructive lesion of the right frontal eye field lets the eyes drift toward the lesion, and right parietal damage brings neglect of the left side of space (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 108). A lesion of the left internal capsule would weaken the right side instead. A pontine lesion would usually bring crossed cranial nerve signs and would not cause neglect, and a lesion of the cervical cord cannot weaken the face.

sections.title: Reading the proportions of a weakness
sections.content:
The motor strip is laid out along the hemisphere like a figure lying upside down over the brain's surface, with the face low on the lateral convexity, the arm and hand above it, and the leg folded over the top onto the medial surface between the hemispheres. The blood supply follows the same geography, since the middle cerebral artery feeds the lateral convexity and so serves the face, arm and tongue, while the anterior cerebral artery feeds the medial surface and so serves the leg (Pearl 2014, p. 7).

**Comparing face, arm and leg**

That layout turns the proportions of a weakness into a measurement that needs nothing but your hands. Grade the face, the arm and the leg separately, and then compare them with one another.

| Pattern | Where |
|---|---|
| Face and arm more than leg | Lateral cortex and the white matter under it: middle cerebral territory |
| Leg more than arm, face spared | Medial cortex near the top of the hemisphere: anterior cerebral territory |
| Face, arm and leg equal | Internal capsule, where the fibres are packed tightly together |

Sources: Pearl 2014, pp. 7, 9-10, 108-109; Brazis 2011, p. 11.

The internal capsule behaves differently for an anatomical reason. In the cortex the fibres for face, arm and leg are spread over a large surface, so a lesion usually catches one part more than another, but by the time they reach the internal capsule they are bundled into a small space, where one small lesion takes all of them equally (Pearl 2014, p. 7).

**The face tells you the level**

Upper motor neuron facial weakness spares the forehead, because the upper face receives cortical input from both sides. A droop of the lower face on the same side as a hemiparesis therefore places the lesion above the upper pons (Brazis 2011, p. 11). If the lower face is spared while the tongue deviates toward the strong side, you should ask whether the weakness is neurological at all (Brazis 2011, p. 12).

**Where the rule bends**

Tumours do not respect vascular territories, and the deficits they cause are untidier and build up over time (Pearl 2014, p. 10). Since most hemispheric lesions in childhood are not strokes, proportion in a child is a guide that you should check against the rest of the story. A focal seizure that marches from the face to the hand to the leg is the homunculus displaying itself in sequence (Pearl 2014, p. 10).
keyPoints: The middle cerebral artery serves the face, arm and tongue, and the anterior cerebral artery serves the leg (Pearl 2014, p. 7).
Face and arm weaker than leg suggests the lateral cortex, leg weaker than arm suggests the medial cortex, and equal weakness of all three suggests the internal capsule.
Upper motor neuron facial weakness spares the forehead, and a lower facial droop on the side of a hemiparesis places the lesion above the upper pons (Brazis 2011, p. 11).
Tumours do not respect vascular territories, so in children proportion is a guide that needs checking (Pearl 2014, p. 10).

question.question: A 14-year-old has a weak right leg, slight clumsiness of the right hand, a normal face and normal speech. The right knee and ankle reflexes are brisk. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: Left medial frontal lobe near the top of the hemisphere
question.explanation: When the leg is much weaker than the arm and the face and speech are spared, the pattern is anterior cerebral, because the leg area lies on the medial surface of the opposite hemisphere (Pearl 2014, pp. 7, 9; Brazis 2011, p. 11). A capsular lesion would weaken face, arm and leg about equally. A lesion of the lateral convexity would weaken the face and arm more than the leg, and on the left it would often disturb language as well. A right medial frontal lesion has the right pattern on the wrong side, since it would weaken the left leg.

sections.title: The visual pathway
sections.content:
Of all the systems in the hemispheres, the visual pathway localizes best, because it runs from the front of the brain to the back and each segment leaves its own signature in the visual field. Three anatomical facts are enough to work out most of those signatures for yourself.

**Three facts**

- **The image is reversed and inverted.** The nasal retina sees the temporal field and the lower retina sees the upper field, and that inversion persists all the way back (Pearl 2014, pp. 26-27).
- **Nasal fibres cross at the chiasm.** Behind the chiasm, each hemisphere carries the opposite half of space from both eyes.
- **Behind the thalamus the fibres fan out.** Those carrying the upper field loop forward through the temporal lobe in Meyer's loop, and those carrying the lower field run through the parietal lobe (Pearl 2014, p. 27).

**The defects that follow**

- Optic nerve: one eye, often with a central scotoma.
- Chiasm: both temporal fields, a bitemporal hemianopia.
- Optic tract: the opposite half-field of both eyes, a homonymous hemianopia.
- Temporal lobe: the opposite upper quadrant.
- Parietal lobe: the opposite lower quadrant.
- Occipital lobe: an opposite homonymous hemianopia, often sparing central vision (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28).

Try each site in the figure above and watch which quadrants go dark.

**Two rules for the occipital lobe**

As the fibres approach the calcarine cortex they gather into tight bundles, so a lesion there affects both eyes alike, and the defect is described as congruous. The macular area also has a dual blood supply, which is why a posterior cerebral infarct often spares central vision. Taken together, the more congruous and the more macula-sparing the defect, the more confidently you can place the lesion in the occipital lobe (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28).

**Testing a child**

Test each eye separately, and watch the child's eyes to make sure they stay on your face. Counting fingers in each quadrant is the best bedside method, while wiggling fingers is easier for children but less sensitive (Pearl 2014, p. 26). In younger children a small toy brought in from the side, or a blink to a threatening hand, can stand in. Presenting stimuli on both sides at once looks for extinction, which is a sign of neglect (Pearl 2014, p. 26). Children rarely complain of a field defect, and the first hint is more often a child who keeps bumping into door frames on one side, or a teacher who notices that the child misses the start of each line.
keyPoints: The retinal image is inverted and the nasal fibres cross, so behind the chiasm each hemisphere sees the opposite half of space (Pearl 2014, pp. 26-27).
A chiasmal lesion gives a bitemporal defect, a tract lesion a homonymous one, a temporal lesion the opposite upper quadrant and a parietal lesion the opposite lower quadrant.
The more congruous and macula-sparing the defect, the more likely the lesion is occipital (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28).
Test each eye separately, prefer finger counting to finger wiggling, and present stimuli on both sides at once to look for extinction (Pearl 2014, p. 26).

question.question: A 12-year-old with headaches is found on confrontation to miss your fingers in the upper left quadrant of both eyes. The defect is roughly similar in each eye but not identical. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: Right temporal lobe, through Meyer's loop
question.explanation: A defect in the same quadrant of both eyes is homonymous, so the lesion lies behind the chiasm, in the hemisphere opposite the missing field, which here is the right. The upper field travels in the lower fibres that loop forward through the temporal lobe, so a right temporal lesion removes the upper left quadrant (Pearl 2014, p. 27). A chiasmal lesion would take both temporal fields, a left parietal lesion would remove the lower right quadrant, and an optic nerve lesion would affect only one eye.

sections.title: Language and the developing brain
sections.content:
In the 1860s Paul Broca argued that language belongs to the left hemisphere, overturning the old assumption that paired organs do identical work (Brazis 2011, p. 1), and the history of localization has been largely the history of aphasia ever since. His central claim still holds in the clinic, where the left hemisphere is dominant for language in almost all right-handed people (Pearl 2014, p. 10).

**Broca's own caution**

Broca also noticed something that a careful localizer should keep in mind. Among his patients, the size of the lesion in the left inferior frontal gyrus did not reliably predict how much speech was lost, so that a small lesion could abolish speech while one many times larger only impaired it (Brazis 2011, p. 1). The map is real, but individual brains differ in how they use it, and that variability is the first form of plasticity anyone described.

**Testing language**

At the bedside it helps to sort language into its parts, which are fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing. A school-aged child can be asked to name pictures, follow a command of several steps, repeat a phrase, read a sentence and write their name, and each pattern of loss points to a different part of the left hemisphere. One famous disconnection shows how literally the map can work. A lesion of the left visual cortex and the corpus callosum leaves a patient able to write but unable to read what they have written (Pearl 2014, p. 28).

**Loss or never gained**

With a child, the first question to ask about language is developmental, and the anatomical question comes after it. A child whose language has always been behind is presumed to have a developmental language disorder unless the story points elsewhere, and that does not localize to a focal lesion. Even the anatomy differs, since the usual leftward enlargement of the inferior frontal gyrus is not found in people with autism or developmental language disorder (Brazis 2011, p. 493). A child who **loses** words they once had, over hours or days, has an acquired aphasia, which is a localizing sign that needs urgent explanation.

**The young brain**

Children injured early in life often regain more language than adults with similar lesions, because the developing brain can reorganise. The recovery is variable, though, and rarely complete in every respect, and since no number we could cite would fit the child in front of you, what you can honestly offer a family is close attention to how their child is doing rather than a percentage.
keyPoints: The left hemisphere is dominant for language in almost all right-handers (Pearl 2014, p. 10).
Broca saw that the size of a lesion did not predict how much speech was lost, which was the first description of cortical plasticity (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Language that was never gained suggests a developmental disorder, whereas language that is lost is an acquired, localizing sign.
Children often recover more language than adults after early injury, but the course is variable, so avoid promising numbers.

question.question: A 5-year-old whose speech was normal for age last week now speaks in short, effortful phrases, cannot name a cup or a key, and has a slightly weak right hand. Which reading is most accurate?
options: An acquired aphasia from a left hemisphere lesion that needs urgent assessment
A developmental language disorder that can be referred for routine speech therapy
A right hemisphere lesion, since the hand weakness is on the right
question.explanation: Language that was present and is now lost, together with a weak right hand, is an acquired aphasia from the left hemisphere, which is dominant for language in almost all right-handers (Pearl 2014, p. 10). That makes it a localizing sign that demands urgent evaluation. A developmental language disorder describes language that was never acquired normally, so it cannot explain speech that has disappeared since last week. A right hemisphere lesion would weaken the left hand. Selective mutism means silence in some settings with normal speech in others, and it does not produce effortful speech, naming errors or focal weakness.

sections.title: Aphasia as four switches
sections.content:
Once you know that a child's language was there and has been lost, the next question is which part of it has gone. The answer still rests on the two addresses from this module's opening, Broca's frontal lobe and Wernicke's temporal lobe, and on the path between them, which Wernicke said could cause aphasia wherever it was cut (Brazis 2011, p. 2).

**Four switches**

Four bedside tests do most of the work (Pearl 2014, pp. 18-20):

- **Fluency:** is speech effortful and sparse, or does it flow?
- **Comprehension:** can the child carry out a spoken command without copying you?
- **Repetition:** can the child say a phrase back word for word?
- **Naming:** can the child name a cup, a key, a shoe?

Set the four switches and the classic syndromes fall out of them (Pearl 2014, p. 20, Table 2.1). Nonfluent speech with understanding preserved is **Broca** aphasia, from the dominant frontal lobe, and fluent speech with understanding lost is **Wernicke** aphasia, from the dominant temporal lobe (Pearl 2014, pp. 18-19). When both are lost the aphasia is **global**, usually from a large lesion. Repetition then divides each of these pairs in two. If repetition survives, the lesion has spared the core and lies in the cortex around it, giving the **transcortical** motor and sensory forms, or a **mixed** form when output and understanding both fail (Pearl 2014, p. 20). Fluent speech and good understanding with failed repetition is **conduction** aphasia, in which talk stays intelligible but carries sound errors and a sentence will not come back intact, and the lesion lies around the supramarginal gyrus or the connection between the language areas (Brazis 2011, p. 524). Even the dominant thalamus can produce aphasia, with a mixed transcortical picture that tends to improve over weeks (Brazis 2011, p. 448; Pearl 2014, p. 20).

Naming fails in almost every row of the table, which is why **anomia** on its own is relatively nonlocalizing (Pearl 2014, p. 20). It tells you that the language network is unwell without telling you where.

**Holding the picture still**

The figure keeps the stimulus fixed, a kite in a tree and a brother on a wobbling ladder, while you flip the switches, so every change in what the child says comes from the lesion you have chosen.

**What aphasia is not**

Slurred speech made of well-built sentences is **dysarthria**, which is a disorder of articulation rather than of language (Pearl 2014, p. 20). A child who falls silent after removal of a cerebellar tumour has **cerebellar mutism**, which should be kept apart from the cortical aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20). A confused, encephalopathic child can also sound aphasic, and the two are hard to separate (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

**Adult rules in a child**

The switches were built from adult patients, so it is unwise to assume that a child's acquired aphasia will sort as neatly, sit where an adult's would, or recover on an adult's schedule. They serve well for describing what you hear and much less well for predicting what will happen.
keyPoints: Fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming are the four bedside tests that sort the aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20, Table 2.1).
Preserved repetition places the lesion in the cortex around the language core, as in the transcortical aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

Fluent speech and good understanding with failed repetition is conduction aphasia (Brazis 2011, p. 524), and a dominant thalamic lesion gives a mixed transcortical picture that improves over weeks (Brazis 2011, p. 448).
Anomia on its own is relatively nonlocalizing (Pearl 2014, p. 20).
Dysarthria, cerebellar mutism after posterior fossa surgery and encephalopathy can all imitate aphasia (Pearl 2014, p. 20).

question.question: A 12-year-old is recovering from a left hemisphere injury. She talks in full sentences at a normal rate and carries out three-step commands. Asked to repeat "the ladder wobbles", she says "the lather... the ladder wobbers" and gives up. Naming is patchy, with sound errors. How do you classify her language, and what does it suggest about the lesion?
options: Broca aphasia, from the dominant inferior frontal lobe
Conduction aphasia, from a lesion around the supramarginal gyrus or the connection between the language areas
Transcortical sensory aphasia, from the cortex around Wernicke's area
Anomic aphasia, which does not localize
question.explanation: Fluent speech and intact comprehension with failed repetition and sound errors is conduction aphasia, which Brazis ties to lesions around the supramarginal gyrus or the pathway linking the language areas (Brazis 2011, p. 524; Pearl 2014, p. 20). Broca aphasia is nonfluent, and she speaks at a normal rate. Transcortical sensory aphasia is the reverse pattern, with understanding lost and repetition kept. Anomic aphasia is tempting because her naming is poor, but it requires repetition to be intact, and repetition is the switch that localizes here. Treat the label as a description, since a child's lesion need not sit exactly where an adult's would.

sections.title: Perinatal brain injury
sections.content:
In the nineteenth century both W. J. Little and Sigmund Freud wrote on the origins of cerebral palsy ([George 1992](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11618412/)), which is the problem of a brain injured before the child has had the chance to do anything with it. Two patterns of early injury are common enough that every child neurologist should recognise them from the examination alone, and in both of them the shape of the deficit reflects where the injury fell.

**The hand that is never chosen**

A stroke around the time of birth often goes unnoticed in the newborn period, and the first sign may be a baby who reaches with only one hand. Hand preference before the first birthday is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand, because true handedness develops only after twelve months ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/home_exam.html)). The child who emerges has a hemiplegic cerebral palsy, with the arm and hand more affected than the leg, a fisted hand, and a leg that circumducts when walking (DeMyer, p. 340). Those are the proportions of the lateral cortex and the middle cerebral territory.

**Legs more than arms**

The premature brain is vulnerable in a different place. Its characteristic injury is periventricular leukomalacia, damage to the white matter around the lateral ventricles, often with injury to neurons and axons as well ([Volpe 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19081519/)). The fibres for the legs pass closest to the ventricles on their way down from the medial cortex, so they are caught first, and the result is spastic diplegia, with severe spasticity in the legs, little in the arms, and little or no trouble with speech or swallowing, which DeMyer contrasts with a double hemiplegia, where the arms are weaker than the legs (DeMyer, p. 340). On their feet these children toe-walk, scissor or walk in a crouch.

**Deep grey matter**

Injury to the basal ganglia and thalamus around birth produces a third pattern, in which involuntary writhing movements are mixed with spasticity (DeMyer, p. 340). The localization of that pattern belongs to the [[m08-loops|loops]], but its timing belongs here.

**The bedside decision**

When an infant shows an early hand preference, examine the neglected hand for tone, reflexes and fisting, and ask about the pregnancy and delivery. When a child born early walks on the toes with stiff legs and good hands, the history and the proportions point to the periventricular white matter before any imaging does. In both cases the examination tells you the level of the injury, and the birth history tells you when it happened.
keyPoints: Hand preference before the first birthday is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Hemiplegic cerebral palsy after perinatal stroke affects the arm more than the leg, with a fisted hand and a circumducting leg (DeMyer, p. 340).
Periventricular leukomalacia is the characteristic white-matter injury of prematurity (Volpe 2009).
Spastic diplegia affects the legs much more than the arms and spares speech and swallowing, whereas in double hemiplegia the arms are weaker than the legs (DeMyer, p. 340).

question.question: A 7-month-old reaches for every toy with the left hand. The right hand is often fisted with the thumb tucked in, and the right arm reflexes are brisker than the left. The pregnancy and birth were uneventful at term. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Early left-handedness, which is normal at this age
Spastic diplegia from periventricular white-matter injury
A right brachial plexus injury from delivery
Right hemiparesis from a left hemisphere injury around the time of birth
question.explanation: Hand preference before the first birthday is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam). A fisted right hand with brisk reflexes is an upper motor neuron sign, which puts the lesion in the left hemisphere, and in a term baby with an uneventful history it fits a perinatal stroke that declared itself late. Early left-handedness is not a real explanation, because handedness is not established this early. Spastic diplegia affects the legs more than the arms and is characteristic of prematurity (Volpe 2009). A brachial plexus injury would give a floppy arm with reduced reflexes rather than a fisted hand with brisk ones.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old has a left homonymous hemianopia that is identical in the two eyes and spares central vision. Where is the lesion?
quiz.explanation: A homonymous defect lies behind the chiasm in the opposite hemisphere, which here is the right. A perfectly congruous defect that spares central vision points to the occipital lobe, where the fibres from the two eyes have come together and the macular area has a dual blood supply (Pearl 2014, pp. 27-28). An optic tract lesion also gives a homonymous hemianopia, but it is usually less congruous and does not spare the macula. A chiasmal lesion removes both temporal fields, and a left occipital lesion would remove the right field.

quiz.question: An 11-year-old has a 30-second episode in which her head and eyes turn forcefully to the left and her left arm jerks. Afterwards she is drowsy. Where does the seizure most likely begin?
quiz.explanation: Each frontal eye field drives the eyes toward the opposite side, and a seizure excites it, so the eyes turn away from the focus and a right frontal seizure drives them to the left (Pearl 2014, p. 9). The jerking left arm points to the right motor strip as well. A destructive right frontal lesion would do the opposite and let the eyes drift to the right, and a left frontal focus would drive them to the right too. Seizures arise in the cortex, so a brainstem origin does not fit.

quiz.question: A 9-year-old has weakness of the right face, arm and leg to the same degree, with no aphasia, no sensory loss and normal visual fields. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
quiz.explanation: Equal weakness of face, arm and leg with no cortical company points to the internal capsule, where the fibres are bundled closely and one small lesion takes them all (Pearl 2014, pp. 7, 109; Brazis 2011, p. 12). A lesion of the lateral convexity would weaken the face and arm more than the leg and, on the left, would often bring aphasia. A medial frontal lesion would weaken the leg more than the rest, and a right capsular lesion would weaken the left side.

quiz.question: A boy born at 28 weeks is now 3. He walks on his toes with stiff, scissoring legs and brisk leg reflexes, but his hands are skilful and his speech is normal for age. What best explains this pattern?
quiz.explanation: Spastic legs with relatively spared arms and normal speech make up spastic diplegia (DeMyer, p. 340), and in a child born very early the characteristic cause is periventricular leukomalacia ([Volpe 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19081519/)), because the leg fibres pass close to the ventricles and are caught first. A middle cerebral stroke would affect one side, and the arm more than the leg. A cerebellar malformation would cause ataxia rather than spasticity, and a neuropathy would reduce the reflexes instead of making them brisk.

quiz.question: Which of these visual field tests is the least sensitive for a mild field defect at the bedside?
options: Counting fingers in each quadrant, one eye at a time
Presenting a red object in each quadrant
quiz.explanation: Counting fingers in each quadrant, with each eye tested separately, is usually the best bedside method, and wiggling fingers, though easier for young children, is less sensitive for mildly reduced vision (Pearl 2014, p. 26). A red object adds sensitivity, because desaturation of red is an early sign of optic nerve disease. Formal perimetry, manual or computerized, is the most sensitive of the four. Finger wiggling still has a place when a child cannot manage anything harder, as long as you remember what it can miss.

quiz.question: A 16-year-old has right arm and face weakness. He understands and follows commands, but his speech is halting and effortful, with few words. Which part of the brain is most likely affected?
quiz.explanation: Halting, effortful, sparse speech with preserved comprehension is the pattern Broca described in lesions of the left inferior frontal gyrus (Brazis 2011, p. 1), and together with right face and arm weakness it fits the lateral cortex of the left hemisphere (Pearl 2014, p. 10). A left posterior temporal lesion would impair comprehension more than fluency. The right hemisphere is rarely dominant for language in a right-hander, and an occipital lesion would affect vision and reading rather than fluency.

quiz.question: A 6-year-old has stopped speaking since removal of a tumour from her cerebellum. She watches faces, carries out simple commands, and moves both arms and legs equally. A trainee writes "global aphasia, ?left hemisphere stroke". How should her silence be framed?
options: Global aphasia from a new left hemisphere stroke, which needs imaging of the left middle cerebral territory before anything else
Selective mutism from the stress of the operation
Broca aphasia, because she is not fluent
Cerebellar mutism, a communication disorder that follows posterior fossa surgery and should not be read as a cortical aphasia
quiz.explanation: Pearl lists cerebellar mutism after posterior fossa surgery, especially after removal of a cerebellar tumour, among the communication problems that must not be confused with the cerebral aphasias (Pearl 2014, p. 20). Her operation was below the tentorium, and a child who understands commands and moves all four limbs equally gives no sign of a large dominant-hemisphere lesion. Global aphasia would take comprehension too and would usually come with right-sided weakness. Calling this Broca aphasia applies the fluency switch to a child who is producing no speech at all, and selective mutism describes silence in some settings with normal speech in others.

opener.parable: The cortex is where localization becomes least precise and most interesting. A lesion there can take away a word, half of the visual world, or a person's awareness that anything is missing at all.
opener.history: In 1865 Paul Broca (1824–1880) wrote that we speak with the left hemisphere, and noticed that a small lesion could abolish speech while a much larger one only dented it. Nine years later Carl Wernicke (1848–1905) placed the understanding of words in the temporal lobe.
